chapters.title: Chapter 5: Using History Without Being Fooled by It

body.text: You cannot predict the cycle, but you can prepare for it. A cycle-aware investor decides in calm times what they will do in euphoric and terrifying times, writes it down, and lets the plan, not the headlines, make the decisions.

children.text: This course has covered three centuries of booms and busts, from tulip contracts in Haarlem to SME IPOs on NSE Emerge. The history is fascinating, but its real value is practical. Across every era, the investors who did well were rarely the ones who called the top or the bottom. They were the ones who expected cycles, avoided the leverage that turns falls into ruin, kept buying when others stopped, and did not bet everything on the story of the moment. This final lesson turns the course into a set of principles and a written plan you can use.

stats.label: Nifty falls of 17% or more
stats.context: In just the decade from 2015 to 2025

stats.label: Sensex long-run growth
stats.context: 1979 to 2024, before dividends, through every one of those falls

body.caption: What market history teaches, and where it came from

cells: 1. Expect cycles
Plan on a 30% to 60% fall in equities at some point in every long investing life. It is normal, not a malfunction
2. Know the engines
Watch credit, interest rates, inflation, commodities and the investment cycle rather than just prices
3. Respect leverage
Borrowed money turns an ordinary fall into a forced sale. Keep margin, F&O and loans against securities out of long-term money
4. Starting valuation sets expectations
Expect less from a market at a P/E near 28 than from one near 12, and adjust gradually, not all at once
5. Leaders rotate
Last cycle's winning sector is rarely the next cycle's. Avoid concentrating in whatever has risen most
6. Diversify
Spread money across asset classes and, where sensible, geographies, because any single market can have a lost decade
7. Test new-era stories
Judge the story and the price separately, and never let a true story justify any price
8. Automate and pre-commit
Use SIPs, rebalancing rules and a written plan so that emotion does not make decisions at extremes

children.text: Step 1: Choose an Allocation You Can Survive

markDefs.definition: How your investments are divided between asset classes such as equity, debt, gold and cash. It is the single biggest driver of how much a portfolio rises and falls.

children.text: The most important cycle decision is made before any cycle arrives: your

. The right mix depends on your goals, time horizon and income stability, but one test matters more than any return projection: could you watch your portfolio fall by the amount in the table below and keep investing? If the honest answer is no, the allocation is too aggressive, because an investor who panics and sells at the bottom does far worse than one with a milder mix who stays the course.

body.caption: Illustrative portfolio falls if equities repeated past crashes (equity fall 60% with debt +8% in a 2008-type crash; equity fall 40% with debt +2% in a 2020-type crash)

body.text: These are simplified illustrations, not the results of any real fund. In a real crash, individual stocks, small caps and sector funds usually fall more than the index, and debt funds are not risk-free either: long-duration funds can lose money when rates rise, and credit-risk funds can suffer in a credit crisis, as the NBFC turmoil of 2018 to 2020 showed. Use the table to test your nerves, not to predict outcomes.

children.text: Lesson 3.4 showed that a steady SIP turns a market that falls and recovers into a gain, because the falls are when the most units get bought. Across the eras in this course, the SIP investor's biggest enemy was never the market. It was the urge to stop in 2009, 2013 and 2020, precisely when their fixed monthly amount was buying the most. For a lump sum, such as a bonus or inheritance, a systematic transfer plan spreads entry over several months, as in the scenario from Lesson 5.1. Use the calculator to see what disciplined monthly investing can build over a full cycle and beyond.
Step 3: Rebalance, the Built-In Cycle Strategy

Rebalancing means bringing your portfolio back to its target mix when markets push it away. It forces you to trim what has risen and add to what has fallen, which is the opposite of what euphoria and panic push you to do. You do not need to predict anything. Here is how it works for an investor with a 60 / 40 equity and debt target and ₹10 lakh invested.

body.title: How Far Did the Boom Push You?
body.prompt: In the table above, after the boom the portfolio holds ₹9 lakh in equity and ₹4.28 lakh in debt. What percentage of the portfolio is now in equity? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Equity share = ₹9 lakh ÷ ₹13.28 lakh ≈ 67.8%. Without doing anything, the investor has drifted from 60% to nearly 68% equity, taking on more risk exactly when valuations are likely higher. Rebalancing back to 60% means selling about ₹1.03 lakh of equity. When the crash comes, the rebalanced portfolio ends about ₹41,000 better off, and rebalancing again after the crash means buying equity when it is cheap.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: What is the main purpose of rebalancing a portfolio back to its target allocation?
options: To guarantee the highest possible return in every market
To keep risk in line with your plan and systematically trim what has risen and add to what has fallen, without needing to predict the market
To avoid ever holding equities during a crash
To follow whichever asset class performed best last year
body.explanation: Rebalancing is a risk control rule first. In a long bull market it can slightly reduce returns, because you keep trimming a rising asset. Its value shows up across full cycles, when it stops a portfolio drifting into excessive risk at tops and forces buying near bottoms. Many investors rebalance once a year, or when an asset class drifts more than about 5 percentage points from target. Consider exit loads and taxes when choosing how to rebalance, for example by redirecting new SIP money rather than selling.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Periodically bringing a portfolio back to its target mix of equity, debt and other assets is called ___.
body.explanation: Rebalancing is the simplest cycle-aware strategy: a mechanical rule that sells a little of what euphoria has inflated and buys a little of what panic has discounted.

children.text: Step 4: Know Your Enemy at Each Stage

body.caption: The cycle, your feelings, and the plan

cells: Euphoria
Everyone is making money, a new-era story explains why it will last
Borrowing, concentrating in hot themes, chasing IPOs
Rebalance, check valuations, keep leverage out, run the new-era checklist
Early decline
"Just a dip, buy it like last time"
Adding leverage or doubling down on the previous leaders
Stick to the allocation, not to last cycle's habits
Panic
Headlines say crash, friends are selling, the portfolio is down 30% or more
Stopping SIPs, selling everything, moving all savings to FDs or gold
Continue SIPs, rebalance into equity, avoid checking the portfolio daily
Grind
Years of little progress, other assets look better
Giving up on equity just before the next up cycle
Remember 2009 to 2013, keep investing, review the engines
Recovery
Scepticism: "This rally won't last"
Waiting for a lower price that never comes
Follow the plan, which has been buying all along

body.title: Two ways to invest through cycles

columns.label: The forecaster
points: Tries to predict the next move from news, tips and charts
Changes allocation based on mood and recent returns
Buys most after rallies, sells most after crashes
Needs to be right twice: when to get out and when to get back in
Often earns less than the funds they own, because of badly timed moves

columns.label: The cycle-aware investor
points: Expects cycles without trying to time them
Sets an allocation based on goals and ability to tolerate falls
Automates investing and rebalances by rule
Uses valuations and cycle engines to adjust expectations and make modest tilts
Captures most of the market's long-run return by staying invested through the cycle

body.title: Write Your Personal Cycle Plan
steps: List your goals, the amount needed, and the year you need each one
Set aside an emergency fund of about six months of expenses in a liquid fund or fixed deposit
Choose a target allocation for each goal, and check it against the illustrative crash table in this lesson
Set up SIPs and decide the date each year when you will review and rebalance, plus a drift band such as 5 percentage points
Write down in advance what you will do if the Nifty falls 20%, 40% and 60%
Write down in advance what you will do if markets rise 50% in a year and everyone around you is euphoric
Keep leverage, F&O and loans against securities out of long-term goal money
Store the plan where you will see it, and read it before making any decision in a boom or a crash

body.title: Final Challenge: One Investor, One Full Cycle
body.scenario: Meera, 32, works in Chennai and invests ₹25,000 a month through SIPs for retirement, with a written plan of 70% equity and 30% debt, and a six-month emergency fund. Over the next four years she faces three moments. Year 1: the market rises 45%, her equity share drifts to 78%, colleagues are borrowing to trade options, and a new theme is "changing everything". Year 2: the Nifty falls 35% in five months, news channels use the word crash daily, and her portfolio is down more than ₹4 lakh. Year 4: the market has been flat for two years, gold has done better, and she wonders if equities were a mistake.
body.prompt: Using the whole course, what should Meera do at each of the three moments, and why?
body.modelAnswer: Year 1, euphoria: Meera should follow her rebalancing rule and bring equity back from 78% to 70%, ideally by directing new SIP money to debt for a while or selling some equity, taking into account exit loads and taxes. She should not borrow or trade options, since leverage is what turns the next fall into ruin, and she should run the new-era checklist on the hot theme, judging the story and the price separately. A market up 45% in a year is also likely trading at higher valuations, so her expectations for the next few years should come down. Year 2, panic: this is the moment the plan was written for. A 35% fall is within the range this course shows happens repeatedly. She should keep every SIP running, because her ₹25,000 now buys far more units, and rebalance back toward 70% equity by moving money from debt into equity, since the fall will have pushed her equity share well below target. Her emergency fund means no job or health shock forces her to sell. Year 4, the grind: two flat years feel like failure, but India's 2009 to 2013 grind showed that a flat index plus steady SIPs can still produce gains, and that switching into the previous cycle's winner, gold then too, is a classic mistake. She should review whether her goals or circumstances have changed. If not, she should keep investing and rebalancing. At every stage the right action came from her written plan, not from predicting the market, which is the whole point of a cycle-aware mindset.

body.title: Course Review: Market Cycles Through History

cards.definition: Earnings drive the long-term trend. Swings in the P/E multiple drive most of the cycle.
Inventory, investment, building and technology cycles run together. The biggest booms and busts come when several turn at once, as in India from 2003 to 2008.
Leverage stretches booms and turns falls into forced sales, from the South Sea Bubble to the 2018 NBFC crisis.
Displacement, boom, euphoria, distress and revulsion.
When the engines stay broken, recovery can take a generation: the Dow after 1929, the Nikkei after 1989, gold after 1980.
The best guide to long-term expected returns, and a poor tool for short-term timing.
Leaders of one era rarely lead the next, so concentration in recent winners is risky.
A survivable allocation, automated SIPs, rules-based rebalancing and pre-written responses to booms and busts.

body.label: SEBI: Check a Registered Investment Adviser
body.description: If you want help building or reviewing your plan, use SEBI's website to confirm that an adviser is a SEBI registered investment adviser before sharing your finances or paying fees.

children.text: Markets will keep moving in cycles, and the next boom will arrive with a new story that sounds more convincing than any in this course. You will not know in advance exactly when it peaks or how far the next fall goes. You do not need to. If you expect the cycle, keep leverage away from your long-term money, keep buying through the falls, rebalance by rule and judge every new era by its price as well as its promise, history suggests you will be one of the investors who comes out ahead.

body.text: The allocation, crash and rebalancing tables in this lesson are simplified illustrations, not recommendations or the results of any real portfolio. The right allocation depends on your personal circumstances, and rebalancing can have tax and exit load costs. Nothing in this course is investment advice. Consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own situation.

points: Market history's core lessons fit into eight principles: expect cycles, know the engines, respect leverage, let valuation set expectations, expect leaders to rotate, diversify, test new-era stories and automate your decisions
Choose an allocation you could survive in a 2008-type crash: roughly −60% for all equity, about −33% for a 60 / 40 mix in a simplified illustration
SIPs and systematic transfer plans turn falls into buying opportunities, but only if you keep going through the panic and the grind
Rebalancing is a built-in cycle strategy: a 60 / 40 portfolio that drifted to about 68% equity after a boom ended about ₹41,000 better off after a crash when rebalanced
Each stage of the cycle has a typical mistake, from borrowing in euphoria to stopping SIPs in panic and quitting equity in the grind
Write your plan in calm times, including what you will do after 20%, 40% and 60% falls, and let the plan make decisions at extremes
